analogy.p: A vector is like a satnav instruction: 'go 3 blocks east and 2 blocks north'. The instruction does not say where you start, just what the journey is, so the same instruction can be followed from anywhere, just like equal vectors drawn in different places. Adding vectors is following one set of directions after another, and the resultant is the single shortcut instruction that does the same job. Going back along a route is the negative of the instruction. The analogy breaks down because a satnav follows roads, whereas vectors are straight-line displacements that ignore obstacles, and a vector does not describe the speed or time taken.

bullets: Magnitude means the length of the vector; direction means which way the arrow points.

Printed vectors use **bold letters** such as **a** or **b**; handwritten vectors are underlined, such as a with a line under it. In an exam always underline your letters so the examiner can see you know they are vectors.
A vector between two points is named with capital letters and an arrow above, such as AB, meaning the displacement **from A to B**.
The arrow on a diagram shows the direction of the vector; the end with the arrowhead is the **head** and the other end is the **tail**.
Equal vectors have the same magnitude and the same direction; they do not need to start at the same point.
The **zero vector** 0 means no movement at all, for example AB + BA = 0.
Examples of vector quantities in real life: displacement, velocity, force. Distance, speed and mass are scalars.
core.p: A **scalar** is a quantity with size only, such as 5 cm, 12 kg or 30 seconds. A **vector** has both **magnitude** (size or length) and **direction**, such as 'move 3 right and 2 up'. In GCSE maths a vector describes a **displacement**: how far and in which direction you move to get from one point to another, with no mention of where you start. This is why two arrows that are the same length and point the same way are **equal vectors**, wherever they are drawn on the page.

bullets: Top number = x-direction (across); bottom number = y-direction (up or down). Never write them with a comma in an exam; stack them in a column inside brackets.
(3 / −2) means 3 to the right and 2 down; (−4 / 1) means 4 to the left and 1 up.
To find the column vector of an arrow from point P to point Q, work out **change in x** and **change in y**: Q minus P. If P = (1, 5) and Q = (4, 2) then PQ = (3 / −3).
The vector in the opposite direction has both signs changed: if PQ = (3 / −3) then QP = (−3 / 3).
Equal column vectors mean equal tops and equal bottoms, so two vector equations can be solved as simultaneous equations.
A **translation** in transformations is described by a column vector, so this idea links straight to the transformations topic.
Do not mix up a column vector (3 / 2) with the coordinate (3, 2): the coordinate is a position, the vector is a movement.
core.p: A **column vector** describes a movement using two numbers written one above the other (in these notes written as (top / bottom)). The **top number** is the horizontal movement: positive means move **right**, negative means move **left**. The **bottom number** is the vertical movement: positive means move **up**, negative means move **down**. So (3 / −2) means 3 right and 2 down. Column vectors let you do vector calculations using simple arithmetic.

bullets: AB = −BA always: reversing direction changes the sign.
If OA = a then AO = −a, because AO runs back from A to O.
A vector written with a single letter, such as a, can be placed anywhere; a vector written with two letters has a fixed start and end.
The direction of a journey along a line is given by the order of the letters, not by the order in which they appear on the page.
AB + BC = AC for any three points A, B and C: going via B gives the same displacement as going straight from A to C.
Check every vector you write by saying it as a journey: 'from A to B' must match the order of your letters.
core.p: The vector AB means the journey from A to B. If you travel the other way you get BA, which has the same length but the opposite direction, so **BA = −AB**. Putting a minus sign in front of a vector reverses its direction without changing its length. Every question that uses a letter pair depends on this idea: if you follow an arrow in its direction you add that vector, and if you go against its arrow you subtract it (or add its negative).

bullets: Head to tail: AB + BC = AC. The 'middle' letter B cancels.
Add column vectors by adding the tops together and adding the bottoms together: (2 / 3) + (4 / −1) = (6 / 2).
Adding is **commutative**: a + b = b + a; the order does not matter for the final vector.
The **parallelogram law**: if two vectors start at the same point, complete the parallelogram; the diagonal from that point is the sum.
Adding the opposite of a vector is the same as taking it away: a + (−a) = 0.
The resultant of several vectors is the single vector that gives the same overall displacement, found by chaining them head to tail.
In 'show that' questions, write each step as a sum such as AB = AO + OB so the examiner can follow your reasoning.
core.p: To add two vectors, place them **head to tail**: draw the first vector, then draw the second starting from the head (arrowhead) of the first. The single arrow from the tail of the first to the head of the second is the **resultant**, which is the sum. This is called the **triangle law**. Adding in a different order gives the same resultant, so a + b = b + a (the parallelogram in the diagrams shows this because both routes arrive at the same point).

bullets: AB = AO + OB = −a + b = b − a. Memorise this: 'end minus start'.
Subtraction is **not** commutative: b − a is the reverse of a − b.
Take care with double negatives in columns: (3 / 1) − (−2 / 4) = (5 / −3).
a − b is the vector from the head of b to the head of a when both start at the same point.
On the parallelogram diagram the second diagonal AB is b − a, the first diagonal OC is a + b.
If you are asked for BA instead of AB then the answer is a − b, the negative of b − a.
Always simplify: for example 3a + 2b − a + b = 2a + 3b.
core.p: To subtract a vector, **add its negative**: a − b = a + (−b). Geometrically, −b is the arrow b reversed. With columns you subtract the tops and subtract the bottoms: (5 / 2) − (1 / 4) = (4 / −2). The most important subtraction in GCSE proofs is finding the vector between two position vectors: if OA = a and OB = b then **AB = −a + b = b − a**, because the journey from A to B goes backwards from A to the origin O, then forwards to B.

bullets: k > 1 stretches the vector; 0 < k < 1 shrinks it; k < 0 reverses it.
2a = a + a, so multiplying by a whole number is repeated addition.
Multiplying by a fraction: (1/3) of (6 / −9) = (2 / −3).
−a is the same length as a but points the opposite way.
Scalar multiplication distributes: 2(a + b) = 2a + 2b, so you can expand and factorise brackets like algebra.
|ka| = |k| × |a|; for example, |−3a| = 3|a|.
Dividing by a number is multiplying by a fraction: a/2 means (1/2)a.
core.h: Multiplying a vector by a scalar
core.p: Multiplying a vector by a **scalar** (an ordinary number) changes its length but not its line of action. 2a is the same direction as a and **twice as long**; (1/2)a is the same direction and half as long; −3a is **opposite** in direction and three times as long. In columns you multiply both numbers by the scalar: 3 × (2 / −1) = (6 / −3). The magnitude of ka is |k| times the magnitude of a.

bullets: Parallel means one vector = k × the other for some number k (k can be negative or a fraction).
Method for parallel vectors: write both in terms of a and b, factorise out a number, and compare what is left in the bracket.
Collinear points A, B, C: show AB = k BC (or AC = k AB). They share the point B, so A, B and C are on the same line.
If AB = 2 BC then A, B, C are collinear and AB is twice the length of BC (and B is between A and C when k is positive and they head the same way).
Never say 'they are the same so they are parallel': say 'the vectors are parallel because one is a multiple of the other'.
Vectors that are not multiples of each other, such as a and b in a triangle, are not parallel; this fact lets you compare coefficients in harder proofs.
Parallel vectors can point in opposite directions (negative scalar multiple).
core.p: Two vectors are **parallel** if one is a **scalar multiple** of the other. For example, 6a + 9b = 3(2a + 3b), so it is parallel to 2a + 3b. To show vectors are parallel, factorise or compare so that one is clearly a multiple of the other. Three or more points are **collinear** (lie on one straight line) if the vectors between them are parallel **and they share a common point**. Parallel on its own is not enough, because parallel lines never meet.

bullets: For (5 / 12) the magnitude is √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13.
For (3 / −4) the magnitude is √(9 + 16) = 5; the signs disappear because squares are positive.
The magnitude of AB is the distance between A and B.
Surd answers: the magnitude of (1 / 2) is √5, which you should leave as a surd unless the question asks for a decimal.
The magnitude of ka is |k| times the magnitude of a, which is a quick check for answers.
Pythagoras triples (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17) appear often in exam vectors, so watch for them.
Do not apply Pythagoras to vectors given in terms of a and b unless you are told their lengths.
core.p: The **magnitude** (length) of a column vector (x / y) is found with **Pythagoras' theorem**: |vector| = √(x² + y²). The two numbers in the column are the legs of a right-angled triangle and the vector is the hypotenuse. Magnitude is always positive or zero, and it is a scalar. Questions often ask you to give the answer as a surd or to 3 significant figures.

bullets: Step 1: write down what the question gives and mark it on the diagram.
Step 2: choose a route from the first letter to the second letter using known vectors or fractions of known vectors.
Step 3: add the vectors along the route, using negatives when going against an arrow.
Step 4: simplify by collecting like terms (a terms with a terms, b terms with b terms).
Example: if OA = a, OB = b, and P is the midpoint of OA, then PB = PO + OB = −(1/2)a + b.
If there are several possible routes the answer is the same, so choose the shortest or the clearest route.
Check by drawing a rough sketch of your answer: the direction should match the diagram.
core.h: Route-finding and writing vectors in terms of a and b
core.p: In an exam diagram you are usually given a few vectors, such as OA = a and OB = b, and must write another vector in terms of them. Find a **route** from the start point to the end point that uses only known vectors. Travelling **with** an arrow adds that vector; travelling **against** an arrow subtracts it. If the route passes a point that divides a line in a ratio, use a fraction of the vector for that part of the line.

bullets: AP : PB = 2 : 3 means 5 equal parts in total, so AP = (2/5)AB and PB = (3/5)AB.
Then OP = a + (2/5)(b − a) = (3/5)a + (2/5)b, as shown in the ratio diagram.
The midpoint is the special case m = n: OM = (1/2)a + (1/2)b.
A line AB can be extended: if P is on AB extended beyond B, then AP is a scalar multiple of AB bigger than 1.
Ratio parts: a ratio 1 : 3 means the dividing point is 1/4 of the way along, not 1/3.
If you know OP = p and OQ = q then PQ = q − p, 'end minus start'.
Always check your fraction of the whole line by saying 'AP is what fraction of AB?'.
core.h: Midpoints and dividing a line in a ratio
core.p: If M is the midpoint of AB then AM = (1/2)AB. If OA = a and OB = b then the **position vector** of M is OM = OA + (1/2)AB = a + (1/2)(b − a) = **(1/2)(a + b)**. For a general point P on AB with **AP : PB = m : n**, the point is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, so AP = (m/(m+n)) AB and OP = (n a + m b)/(m + n). Always start with the fraction of the whole line rather than trying to guess the answer.

bullets: Write down the vectors you are given first.
Work out the two vectors you need to compare using a clear route, showing each step.
Simplify and factorise so the relationship is obvious, for example OQ = 2(2a + b).
To prove lines are parallel: show one vector is a scalar multiple of the other.
To prove points are collinear: show the vectors are parallel **and** share a common point.
To prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram: show one pair of opposite sides is equal and parallel, for example AB = DC.
To prove M is a midpoint: show AM = MB, or show AM = (1/2)AB with the same direction.
Finish: 'Therefore ... because ...' using the exact reason.
core.p: A **vector proof** is a short logical argument written in vectors that ends with a clear statement. The most common conclusions are 'the lines are **parallel**', 'the points are **collinear**', 'M is the **midpoint**' or 'the shape is a **parallelogram**'. You must show the working in steps, use the correct reasoning words, and finish with a conclusion in words that answers the question. Without the final sentence you can lose the communication mark.

bullets: Find two vectors that join the points, both written in terms of a and b.
Factorise out numbers: for example 6a + 9b = 3(2a + 3b).
Spot the multiple: 'one is k times the other'.
State the common point: two vectors that start at the same letter share a point, so the lines meet there.
Conclude with the geometrical statement in words, such as 'so A, B and C are collinear'.
If you cannot get a multiple, check your algebra: arithmetic slips in fractions are the commonest reason the proof fails.
Do not rely on diagrams: diagrams in vector questions are often not drawn accurately.
core.h: Proof: showing points are collinear (worked pattern)
core.p: Suppose you are asked to show that three points P, Q and R lie on a straight line. Work out PQ and PR (or PQ and QR) in terms of a and b. Simplify both. If one is a multiple of the other, say 'PR = 3PQ, so PQ and PR are parallel. They share the point P so P, Q, R are on a straight line.' The same pattern shows that two sides of a figure are parallel without needing the common point.

bullets: Expand: 3(2a − b) = 6a − 3b.
Collect: 4a + 2b − a + 5b = 3a + 7b.
Factorise to show a multiple: 8a − 12b = 4(2a − 3b).
You cannot simplify a + b to 'ab' or '2ab': they are different vectors.
Use brackets around negative sums: −(a − b) = −a + b = b − a.
If you get stuck, replace a and b with simple column vectors to test your expression.
core.h: Algebra skills needed for vector work
core.p: Vector manipulation uses the same rules as algebra: you expand brackets, collect like terms and factorise, treating a and b like letters. The important difference is that a and b are vectors, so you cannot multiply two vectors together at GCSE, and you cannot combine an a-term with a b-term. Fractions often appear, so be careful with common denominators and with negative fractions.

bullets: Equate coefficients: if xa + yb = 3a + 5b and a, b are not parallel, then x = 3 and y = 5.
Write each route with a letter such as h or k as an unknown fraction, then solve the simultaneous equations.
Vectors with a sum of zero make a closed shape: for a triangle, AB + BC + CA = 0.
Transformations: a translation is a movement described by a column vector.
Ratio: points dividing lines use the ratio ideas to give fractions of vectors.
Similar triangles: MN parallel to AB gives similar triangles with scale factor 1/2 in the midpoint theorem.
Area ratio: if lengths are in ratio 1 : 2 then areas of similar shapes are in ratio 1 : 4.
Bearings and trigonometry may be needed if vectors are given as lengths and angles.
core.h: Comparing coefficients: harder proofs and links to other topics
core.p: In the hardest questions, a point is reached by two different routes. For example, X is on OA and on BP, so you write OX in two ways, both in terms of a and b, and equate. Because a and b are **not parallel**, the numbers in front of a must match on both sides, and the numbers in front of b must match. This gives simultaneous equations to solve. Vectors also link to coordinate geometry, ratio, similar triangles and translations in transformations.

exam: Command words: **Find**, **write down**, **express ... in terms of a and b** (find a vector expression); **show that** / **prove** (structured argument ending in a conclusion); **explain** (give the reason in words).
Typical mark allocations: 1 to 2 marks for one vector expressed using a route; 3 to 4 marks for midpoints or ratio; 4 to 6 marks for full proofs.
For one-step 'express in terms of a and b' questions, show the route, such as AB = AO + OB = −a + b, to earn the method mark even if you slip.
In Edexcel mark schemes, M marks are for method, A marks for accuracy and C marks for communication (clear reasoning and conclusion).
Write vector letters underlined in handwriting; if the question uses bold, mirror its notation.
For proofs always finish with a sentence: 'Therefore ... are parallel / collinear because ...'.
'Show that' means you must show every step; do not just state the answer.
Simplify fully: collect like terms and give fractions in simplest form, e.g. (1/2)a + (3/2)b.
If the ratio is given, convert it to a fraction of the whole line before writing a vector.
Use a quick sketch even if a diagram is given, marking known vectors with arrows in the correct direction.
Check your answer by re-deriving it via a second route if time allows.
Magnitude questions: show the squares and square root, √(x² + y²), and leave in surd form if asked for exact.

mistakes.r: AB = −a + b = b − a (end minus start); AB = AO + OB.
mistakes.w: Writing AB = a + b when OA = a and OB = b.

mistakes.r: Travelling against a vector subtracts it, so AO = −a.
mistakes.w: Forgetting that going against the arrow gives a negative.

mistakes.r: Vectors must be shown as underlined letters (or bold in print) so the examiner knows they are vectors.
mistakes.w: Not underlining vector letters in handwriting, or writing them like ordinary algebra.

mistakes.r: Parallel vectors are collinear only if they also share a common point; say both.
mistakes.w: Saying 'they are parallel so they are collinear'.

mistakes.r: Add tops to tops and bottoms to bottoms.
mistakes.w: Adding the wrong way for column vectors, for example adding a top to a bottom.

mistakes.r: 2 : 3 has 5 parts, so the point is 2/5 of the way along.
mistakes.w: Using the ratio 2 : 3 as 2/3 of the line.

mistakes.r: Terms in a and terms in b stay separate: 2a + 3b.
Check each line; a correct proof arrives at the result naturally. Do not fake the last line.
mistakes.w: Making an arithmetic error in the middle of a proof and forcing the answer.

mistakes.r: State the result in words: 'so A, B and C are collinear' or 'so MN is parallel to AB'.
mistakes.w: Leaving a vector proof without a conclusion.

summary: You must be able to add and subtract vectors, multiply them by a scalar, and work with them both as arrows (diagrams) and as column vectors, then use them to build geometric arguments and proofs. This is a Higher tier skill: typical questions give OA = a and OB = b and ask you to write other vectors in terms of a and b, then prove that lines are parallel, that points are collinear, or that a point is a midpoint. It matters because it is a regular high-mark (4 to 6 mark) question at the end of Paper 1, 2 or 3 and it tests algebra, geometry and reasoning together.

svg.cap: Split AB into 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts. P is 2 parts from A, so AP = 2/5 AB. Always start from a known position vector and add the fraction of AB.

terms.d: A quantity with magnitude (size) only, such as a number or a length.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction.
The size or length of a vector.
A vector written as two numbers in a column; the top number is the horizontal movement and the bottom number is the vertical movement.
The single vector that is the sum of two or more vectors.
The vector from a fixed origin O to a point, for example OA.
A vector multiplied by a number; the result is parallel to the original vector.
Vectors where one is a scalar multiple of the other, so they have the same direction or exactly opposite directions.
Points that lie on the same straight line.
The vector with the same magnitude but opposite direction; −a is the negative of a.
The vector 0, with magnitude zero and no direction, for example AB + BA.
The rule that vectors are added by placing them head to tail, so AB + BC = AC.
The point halfway along a line segment; for M the midpoint of AB, AM = (1/2)AB.
A change in position, given by a distance and a direction.
A logical argument that shows a statement is always true, ending in a clear conclusion.
Vectors with the same magnitude and the same direction.

worked.ans: (a) (2 / 9); (b) (6 / −8); (c) 10; (d) (6 / −8) = 2(3 / −4), a scalar multiple, so they are parallel.
worked.q: (5 marks) p = (4 / −3) and q = (−2 / 5). (a) Work out 2p + 3q. (b) Work out p − q. (c) Work out the magnitude of p − q. (d) Show that p − q is parallel to (3 / −4).
steps: (d) (6 / −8) = 2 × (3 / −4). It is a scalar multiple, so the vectors are parallel.

worked.ans: (a) AB = b − a. (b) OM = a + (1/2)(b − a) = (1/2)(a + b), as required.
worked.q: (4 marks) OAB is a triangle. OA = a and OB = b. M is the midpoint of AB. (a) Find AB in terms of a and b. (b) Show that OM = (1/2)(a + b).
steps: (a) AB = AO + OB = −a + b = b − a.
(b) AM = (1/2)AB because M is the midpoint, so AM = (1/2)(b − a).

worked.ans: OQ = 2OP, so OP and OQ are parallel. They share the point O, therefore O, P and Q are collinear (P is the midpoint of OQ).
worked.q: (5 marks) OAB is a triangle with OA = 3a and OB = 3b. P is the point on AB such that AP : PB = 1 : 2. Q is the point such that OQ = 4a + 2b. Prove that O, P and Q are collinear.
steps: AP = (1/3)AB because AP : PB = 1 : 2 gives 1 part out of 3. So AP = (1/3)(3b − 3a) = b − a.
OP = OA + AP = 3a + b − a = 2a + b.
OQ is a scalar multiple of OP, so OP and OQ are parallel, and they share the point O.
